title: Direct and inverse variation
log: 2026-11-01T08:04:34Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The new point covers both direct and inverse variation and asks students to recognise each from a table, graph or rule, but the bank's direct variation point teaches only direct variation and its inverse variation point teaches only inverse variation at Year 12 depth, so neither matches.

draft.title: Direct and inverse variation
card: y = kx, where k is a constant. When x doubles, y doubles. The graph is a straight line through the origin.
y = k/x, where k is a constant. When x doubles, y halves. The graph is a curve that falls and never touches either axis.
From a table, test the pattern. In direct variation y ÷ x is always the same. In inverse variation x × y is always the same.
Example: x = 2, 4, 5 and y = 20, 10, 8. Here x × y = 40 every time, so y = 40/x and the variation is inverse.
draft.remember: Direct: y ÷ x stays constant. Inverse: x × y stays constant.

a.q: A table gives x = 2, 4, 6 and y = 6, 12, 18. Which rule fits?
a.why: Each y ÷ x equals 3, so y = 3x and the variation is direct. The rule y = 12/x is tempting because 12 appears in the table, but x × y is not constant: 2 × 6 = 12 and 4 × 12 = 48.
a.clue: Divide each y by its x and compare.

b.q: Cars on a road travel the same 120 km. Time taken t hours varies with speed v km/h as t = 120/v. What happens to t when v is doubled?
b.why: The rule is inverse variation, so doubling v halves t. Doubling t would be direct variation, which is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: Is the rule y = kx or y = k/x?

check.summary: No problems found. The card's facts and example check out, and each question has exactly one correct option, which matches the writer's explanations.
